etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English court, from Old French cort, curt, from Latin cōrtem (accusative of cōrs), ultimately from cohors. Doublet of cohort.

definitions.definition: (Australia, US) A street with no outlet, a cul-de-sac.
(Hong Kong, only used in names) A housing estate under the Home Ownership Scheme.
(Hong Kong, only used in names) An apartment building, or a small development of several apartment buildings.
An enclosed space; a courtyard; an uncovered area shut in by the walls of a building, or by different buildings; also, a space opening from a street and nearly surrounded by houses; a blind alley.

quote.citation: 1832 December (indicated as 1833), Alfred Tennyson, “The Palace of Art”, in Poems, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, stanza XXX, page 77:
quote.text: All round the cool green courts there ran a row / Of cloisters, branched like mighty woods, / Echoing all night to that sonorous flow / Of spouted fountain floods.

quote.citation: 1856 February, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Oliver Goldsmith”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: Goldsmith took a garret in a miserable court.

definitions.definition: The residence of a sovereign, prince, nobleman, or other dignitary; a palace.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: This our court, infected with their manners, / Shows like a riotous inn.

definitions.definition: The collective body of persons composing the retinue of a sovereign or person high in authority; all the surroundings of a sovereign in his regal state.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: My lord, there is a nobleman of the court at door would speak with you.

quote.citation: 1819–1824, [Lord Byron], Don Juan, London, (please specify |canto=I to XVII):
quote.text: Love rules the court, the camp, the grove.

definitions.definition: Any formal assembling of the retinue of a sovereign.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter XX, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: The princesses […]  held their court within the fortress.

definitions.definition: (social) Royal society.
Attention directed to a person in power; behaviour designed to gain favor; politeness of manner; civility towards someone

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto II”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: No solace could her paramour entreat / Her once to show, ne court, nor dalliance.

quote.citation: 1667 April 28 (Gregorian calendar), John Evelyn, “[Diary entry for 18 April 1667]”, in William Bray, editor, Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn, […], 2nd edition, volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […]; and sold by John and Arthur Arch, […], published 1819, →OCLC:
quote.text: I went to make court to the Duke and Duchess of Newcastle at their house in Clerkenwell.

definitions.definition: The hall, chamber, or place, where justice is administered.

The persons officially assembled under authority of law, at the appropriate time and place, for the administration of justice; an official assembly, legally met together for the transaction of judicial business; a judge or judges sitting for the hearing or trial of cases.

quote.citation: 2012 August 21, Ed Pilkington, “Death penalty on trial: should Reggie Clemons live or die?”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: Next month, Clemons will be brought before a court presided over by a "special master", who will review the case one last time. The hearing will be unprecedented in its remit, but at its core will be a simple issue: should Reggie Clemons live or die?

quote.citation: 1985, “Criminal Code (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46)”, in Justice Canada‎[1], retrieved 1 March 2020:
quote.text: 536(2.1). ... You have the option to elect to be tried by a provincial court judge without a jury; or you may elect to be tried by a judge without a jury; or you may elect to be tried by a court composed of a judge and jury.

definitions.definition: An organization for the administration of law, consisting of a body of judges with a certain jurisdiction along with its administrative apparatus.
(often capitalized) The judge or judges or other judicial officer presiding in a particular matter, particularly as distinguished from the counsel or jury, or both.

quote.citation: 2017 May 5, Kevin R. Aalto, “Gordon v. Canada, 2017 FC 454”, in CanLII‎[2], retrieved 23 February 2020:
quote.text: A case conference in person was convened.... To emphasize that it was a Court proceeding the Court was gowned.

quote.citation: 2018 August 17, M.F. McParland, “R. v. Carlson, 2018 BCPC 209”, in CanLII‎[3], retrieved 1 March 2020:
quote.text: [5]... defence alleges there is a reasonable apprehension of bias based on the cumulative effect of several issues including the following: (1) The Court was “crying” during the victim impact statement; (2) The Court laughed or “scoffed” when defence stated its sentencing position; ...(6) The Court’s tone, facial expression and demeanor throughout the proceedings...

definitions.definition: The session of a judicial assembly.

quote.citation: 2023 February 16, WCCO Staff, “Julissa Thaler sentenced to life in prison for murdering 6-year-old son, Eli Hart”, in cbsnews.com‎[4]:
quote.text: On Thursday morning, a Hennepin County judge formally sentenced Julissa Thaler to the life sentence for Eli Hart's murder.  […]  After court, family said their focus now turns to fundraising a playground in Mound in Eli Hart's honor  […]

definitions.definition: Any jurisdiction, civil, military, or ecclesiastical.
(law) The administration of law.
one of the two divisions of a tennis, badminton or volleyball court, in which the player or players of each team play

quote.citation: 2010, Cara Marcus, Faulkner Hospital:
quote.text: The photograph at left captures a great serve by Dr. Sadowsky, who will never forget one of Bobby Riggs's serves, which had such a great spin that it landed in his court and bounced back to the other side of the net before he had a chance to return it.

definitions.definition: (sports) A place arranged for playing the games of tennis, basketball, handball, badminton, volleyball, squash and some other games

quote.citation: 1935, George Goodchild, chapter 5, in Death on the Centre Court:
quote.text: By one o'clock the place was choc-a-bloc. […] The restaurant was packed, and the promenade between the two main courts and the subsidiary courts was thronged with healthy-looking youngish people, drawn to the Mecca of tennis from all parts of the country.

definitions.definition: (ornithology) A space prepared and decorated by certain bird species in which to advertise themselves for a mate.
(transitive) To seek to achieve or win (a prize).

quote.citation: 1800, William H[ickling] Prescott, History of The Reign of Philip The Second, King of Spain, volume 3:
quote.text: On the contrary, they employed the brief respite that was left them in fortifying one another's courage, and in bearing testimony to the truth in so earnest a manner that they might almost seem to have courted the crown of martyrdom.

quote.citation: 1821, Thomas De Quincey, “To the Reader”, in Confessions of an English Opium-Eater:
quote.text: Guilt and misery shrink, by a natural instinct, from public notice: they court privacy and solitude: and even in their choice of a grave will sometimes sequester themselves from the general population of the churchyard  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To risk (a consequence, usually negative).

quote.citation: 1964 April, “Automatic Signalling Problems in an Emergency”, in Modern Railways, page 273:
quote.text: It is not unknown for hot axleboxes to fail completely and for wagons to become derailed as a result. Surely it is courting disaster to allow a train to proceed for up to seven miles with a defective vehicle before it can be brought to a halt?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To try to win a commitment to marry from.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592, William Shakespeare, The Taming of the Shrew, act 1, scene 1:
quote.text: If either of you both love Katharina  […]  / Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To engage in behavior conducive to mating with.

quote.citation: 1849, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter 24, in The History of England: From the Accession of James II, volume 5:
quote.text: By one person, however, Portland was still assiduously courted, and that person was the king.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To attempt to attract; to invite by attractions; to allure.

quote.citation: a. 1835, Alfred Lord Tennyson, The Gardener's Daughter:
quote.text: […]  a well-worn pathway courted us / To one green wicket in a privet hedge  […]

quote.citation: 1902, Robert Marshall Grade, The Haunted Major:
quote.text: It is a grim, grey old town, standing on bleak, precipitous cliffs that court every passing hurricane,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To attempt to gain alliance with.
(intransitive) To engage in activities intended to win affections.
(intransitive) To engage in courtship behavior.
